transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: Hello, Junior Cycle camp, Jake speaking.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Hi. I'm calling for some information about the cycle camp – I'm thinking of sending my son.

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: Great. Well, it's held every weekday morning over the summer vacation and we focus on basic cycling skills and safety. We have eight levels for children from three years upwards. How old's your son?

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Charlie? He's seven. He can ride a bike, but he needs a little more training before he's safe to go on the road.

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: He'd probably be best in Level 5. They start off practising on the site here, and we aim to get them riding on the road, but <q id="1">first they're taken to ride in the park,</q> away from the traffic.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Right. And can you tell me a bit about the instructors?

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: Well, all our staff wear different coloured shirts. So, we have three supervisors, and they have red shirts. They support the instructors, and they also stand in for me if I'm not around. Then <q id="2">the instructors themselves are in blue shirts,</q> and one of these is responsible for each class.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: OK.

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: In order to be accepted, all our instructors <q id="3">have to submit a reference</q> from someone who's seen them work with children – like if they've worked as a babysitter, for example. Then they have to complete our training course, including how to do lesson plans, and generally care for the well-being of the kids in their class. They do a great job, I have to say.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Right. And tell me a bit about the classes. What size will Charlie's class be?

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: We have a limit of eight children in each class, so their instructor really gets to know them well. They're out riding most of the time but they have <q id="4">quiet times too, where their instructor might tell them a story</q> that's got something to do with cycling, or get them to play a game together. It's a lot of fun.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: It must be. Now, <q id="5">what happens if there's rain? Do the classes still run?</q>

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: <q id="5">Oh yes. We don't let that put us off</q> – we just put on our waterproofs and keep cycling.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: And is there anything special Charlie should bring along with him?

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: Well, maybe some spare clothes, especially if the weather's not so good. And <q id="6">a snack</q> for break time.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: How about a drink?

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: No, we'll provide that. And make sure he has shoes, not sandals.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Sure. And just at present <q id="7">Charlie has to take medication every few hours, so I'll make sure he has that.</q>

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: Absolutely. Just give us details of when he has to take it and we'll make sure he does.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: Now, there are a few things you should know about Day 1 of the camp. The classes normally start at 9.30 every morning, but on Day 1 you should aim to get Charlie here by 9.20. The finishing time will be 12.30 as usual. We need the additional time because there are a few extra things to do. The most important is that we have a very careful <q id="8">check to make sure that every child's helmet fits properly.</q> If it doesn't fit, we'll try to adjust it, or we'll find him another one – but he must wear it all the time he's on the bike.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Of course.

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: Then after that, all the instructors will be waiting to meet their classes, and <q id="9">they'll meet up in the tent</q> – you can't miss it. And each instructor will take their class away and get started.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: OK. Well that all sounds good. Now can you tell me how much the camp costs a week?

transcript.speaker: JAKE
transcript.text: <q id="10">One hundred ninety-nine dollars.</q> We've managed to keep the price more or less the same as last year – it was one hundred ninety then. But the places are filling up quite quickly.

transcript.speaker: WOMAN
transcript.text: Right. OK, well I'd like to book for ...
Hello everyone. My name's Megan Baker and I'm a recruitment consultant at AVT Recruitment specialists.

Now, our company specialises in positions that involve working in the agriculture and horticulture sectors, so that's fresh food production, garden and park maintenance and so on. And these sectors do provide some very special career opportunities. For a start, they often offer <q id="11">opportunities for those who don't want to be stuck with a 40-hour week, but need to juggle work with other responsibilities</q> such as child care – and this is very important for many of our recruits. Some people like working in a rural setting, surrounded by plants and trees instead of buildings, although we can't guarantee that. But there are <q id="12">certainly health benefits, especially in jobs where you're not sitting all day looking at a screen</q> – a big plus for many people. Salaries can sometimes be good too, although there's a lot of variety here. And you may have the opportunity in some types of jobs for travel overseas, although that obviously depends on the job, and not everyone is keen to do it.

Of course, working outdoors does have its challenges. It's fine in summer, but <q id="13">can be extremely unpleasant when it's cold and windy.</q> You may need to be pretty fit for some jobs, though with modern technology that's not as important as it once was. And standards of health and safety are much higher now than they used to be, so there are fewer work-related accidents. But <q id="14">if you like a lively city environment surrounded by lots of people, these jobs are probably not for you – they're often in pretty remote areas.</q> And some people worry about finding a suitable place to live, but in our experience, this usually turns out fine.
Now let me tell you about some of the exciting jobs that we have on our books right now.

One is for a fresh food commercial manager. Our client here is a very large fresh food producer supplying a range of top supermarkets. They operate in a <q id="15">very fast-paced environment</q> with low profit margins – the staff there <q id="15">work hard, but they play hard as well,</q> so if you've a sociable personality this may be for you.

We have an exciting post as an agronomist advising farmers on issues such as crop nutrition, protection against pests, and the latest legislation on farming and agricultural practices. There are <q id="16">good opportunities for the right person to quickly make their way up the career ladder,</q> but a deep knowledge of the agricultural sector is expected of applicants.

A leading supermarket is looking for a fresh produce buyer who is available for a <q id="17">12-month maternity cover</q> contract. You need to have experience in administration, planning and buying in the fresh produce industry, and in return will receive a very competitive salary.

We have also received a request for a sales manager for a chain of garden centres. You will <q id="18">be visiting centres in the region</q> to ensure their high levels of customer service are maintained. This post is only suitable for someone who is prepared to live in the region.

There is also a vacancy for a tree technician to carry out tree cutting, forestry and conservation work. Candidates must have a clean driving licence and have training in safety procedures. A year's experience would be preferred but <q id="19">the company might be prepared to consider someone who has just completed an appropriate training course.</q>

Finally, we have a position for a farm worker. This will involve a wide range of farm duties including crop sowing and harvesting, machine maintenance and animal care. Perks of the job include <q id="20">the possibility of renting a small cottage on the estate,</q> and the chance to earn a competitive salary. A driving licence and tractor driving experience are essential.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: OK Rosie, shall we try to get some ideas together for our presentation on diet and obesity?

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: I can talk about the experiment I did to see if people can tell the difference between real sugar and artificial sweeteners.

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Where you gave people drinks with either sugar or artificial sweeteners and they had to say which they thought it was?

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: Yeah. It took me ages to decide exactly how I'd organise it, especially how I could make sure that <q id="21">people didn't know which drink I was giving them.</q> It was hard to keep track of it all, especially as <q id="22">I had so many people doing it</q> – I had to make sure I kept a proper record of what each person had had.

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: So could most people tell the difference?

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: Yeah – I hadn't thought they would be able to, but most people could.

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Then there's that experiment I did measuring the fat content of nuts, to see if the nutritional information given on the packet was accurate.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: The one where you ground up the nuts and mixed them with a chemical to absorb the fat?

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Yes. My results were a bit problematic – the fat content for that type of nut seemed much lower than it said on the package. But I reckon the package information was right. I think <q id="23">I should probably have ground up the nuts more than I did.</q> <q id="24">It's possible that the scales for weighing the fat weren't accurate enough,</q> too. I'd really like to try the experiment again some time.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: So what can we say about helping people to lose weight? There's a lot we could say about what restaurants could do to reduce obesity. I read that the items at the start of a menu and the items at the end of a menu are much more likely to be chosen than the items in the middle. So, <q id="25">if you put the low-calorie items at the beginning and end of the menu, people will probably go for the food with fewer calories,</q> without even realising what they're doing.

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: I think food manufacturers could do more to encourage healthy eating.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: How?

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Well, <q id="26">when manufacturers put calorie counts of a food on the label, they're sometimes really confusing and I suspect they do it on purpose.</q> Because food that's high in calories tastes better, and so they'll sell more.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: Yeah, so if you look at the amount of calories in a pizza, they'll give you the calories per quarter pizza and you think, oh that's not too bad. But who's going to eat a quarter pizza?

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: I suppose another approach to this problem is to get people to exercise more.

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Right. In England, the current guidelines are for at least 30 minutes of brisk walking, five days a week. Now when you ask them, <q id="27">about 40% of men and 30% of women say they do this, but when you objectively measure the amount of walking they do with motion sensors, you find that only 6% of men and 4% of women do the recommended amount of exercise.</q>

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: Mm, so you can see why obesity is growing.

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: So how can people be encouraged to take more exercise?

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: Well, for example, think of the location of stairs in a train station. <q id="28">If people reach the stairs before they reach the escalator when they're leaving the station, they're more likely to take the stairs.</q> And <q id="28">if you increase the width of the stairs, you'll get more people using them at the same time. It's an unconscious process and influenced by minor modifications in their environment.</q>

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Right. And it might not be a big change, but if it happens every day, it all adds up.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: Yes. But actually, <q id="29">I'm not sure if we should be talking about exercise in our presentation.</q>

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: Well, we've done quite a bit of reading about it.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: I know, but it's going to mean we have a very wide focus, and our tutor did say that <q id="29">we need to focus on causes and solutions in terms of nutrition.</q>

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: <q id="29">I suppose so. And we've got plenty of information about that. OK,</q> well that will be simpler.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: So what shall we do now? We've still got half an hour before our next lecture.

transcript.speaker: ROSIE
transcript.text: <q id="30">Let's think about what we're going to include and what will go where.</q> Then we can decide what slides we need.

transcript.speaker: ADAM
transcript.text: OK, fine.

Good morning everyone. So today we're going to look at an important creative activity and that's hand knitting. Ancient knitted garments have been found in many different countries, showing that knitting is a global activity with a long history.

When someone says the word 'knitting' <q id="31">we might well picture an elderly person – a grandmother perhaps – sitting by the fire knitting</q> garments for themselves or other members of the family. It's a homely image, but one that may lead you to feel that knitting is an activity of the past – and, indeed, <q id="32">during the previous decade, it was one of the skills that was predicted to vanish</q> from everyday life. For although humans have sewn and knitted their own clothing for a very long time, many of these craft-based skills went into decline when industrial machines took over – mainly because they were no longer passed down from one generation to another. However, that's all changing and interest in knitting classes in many countries is actually rising, as more and more people are seeking formal instruction in the skill. With that trend, we're also seeing <q id="33">an increase in the sales figures for knitting equipment.</q>

So why do people want to be taught to knit at a time when a machine can readily do the job for them? The answer is that knitting, as a handicraft, has numerous benefits for those doing it. Let's consider what some of these might be. While many people knitted garments in the past because they couldn't afford to buy clothes, it's still true today that <q id="34">knitting can be helpful if you're experiencing economic hardship.</q> If you have several children who all need warm winter clothes, knitting may save you a lot of money. And the results of knitting your own clothes can be very rewarding, even though <q id="35">the skills you need to get going are really quite basic</q> and the financial outlay is minimal.

But the more significant benefits in today's world are to do with well-being. In a world where it's estimated that we spend up to nine hours a day online, doing something with our hands that is craft-based makes us feel good. It releases us from the stress of a technological, fast-paced life.
Now, let's look back a bit to early knitting activities. In fact, no one really knows when knitting first began, but archaeological remains have disclosed plenty of information for us to think about.

One of the interesting things about knitting is that the earliest pieces of clothing that have been found suggest that <q id="36">most of the items produced were round</q> rather than flat. Discoveries from the 3rd and 4th centuries in Egypt show that things like socks and gloves, that were needed to keep hands and feet warm, were knitted in one piece using four or five needles. That's very different from most knitting patterns today, which only require two. What's more, the very first needles people used were hand carved out of wood and <q id="37">other natural materials, like bone,</q> whereas today's needles are largely made of steel or plastic and make that characteristic clicking sound when someone's using them. Ancient people knitted using yarns made from linen, hemp, cotton and wool, and <q id="38">these were often very rough on the skin.</q> The spinning wheel, which allowed people to make finer yarns and produce much greater quantities of them, led to the dominance of wool in the knitting industry – often favoured for its warmth.

Another interesting fact about knitting is that because it was practised in so many parts of the world for so many purposes, <q id="39">regional differences in style developed.</q> This visual identity has allowed researchers to match bits of knitted clothing that have been unearthed over time to the region from which the wearer came or the job that he or she did.

As I've mentioned, knitting offered people from poor communities a way of making extra money while doing other tasks. For many centuries, it seems, men, women and children took every opportunity to knit, for example, while <q id="40">watching over sheep,</q> walking to market or riding in boats.
